evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected acute stroke in the emergency department: recognition, imaging, thrombolysis, thrombectomy referral and early care. Verified against NICE NG128, the European Stroke Organisation IV thrombolysis guideline (2021) and the alteplase prescribing information. No Saudi national stroke guideline was found in open sources; follow the local stroke-code protocol.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: Ischaemic stroke is sudden focal neurological loss from arterial occlusion (thrombosis or embolism). Around the irreversibly infarcted core lies the ischaemic penumbra — tissue that can be saved if blood flow is restored quickly, which is why treatment is time-critical.
keyMechanisms: Causes: large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism (atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis), small-vessel (lacunar) disease, arterial dissection and other rarer causes.

Penumbra survival falls with every minute of occlusion; thrombolysis and thrombectomy aim to reperfuse it. Advanced imaging (CT perfusion or MRI) identifies salvageable tissue beyond standard time windows.
Thrombolysis risks symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage — hence strict exclusion of haemorrhage on CT and control of BP to 185/110 mmHg or lower.
Hyperglycaemia, hypoxaemia and fever worsen the injury; aspiration is common with dysphagia.

symptoms: Sudden facial weakness, arm or leg weakness, speech disturbance (FAST).
Visual field loss, diplopia, vertigo, ataxia (posterior circulation).
Severe headache at onset, vomiting or reduced consciousness suggest haemorrhage.
physicalSigns: Focal deficit — use ROSIER in the ED and record NIHSS for treatment decisions.
Irregular pulse (AF), carotid bruit, murmurs (embolic source).
BP often raised; check glucose immediately (hypoglycaemia mimics stroke).
redFlags: Last known well within 4.5 h → stroke code, immediate CT
Severe deficit — possible large vessel occlusion → CTA for thrombectomy
Anticoagulant use, bleeding tendency, GCS below 13, fluctuating symptoms, severe headache, fever/neck stiffness → immediate CT

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Only reliably excluded by CT; manage BP and reverse anticoagulation (NICE).
Witnessed seizure; ESO suggests IVT if no suspicion of mimic or head trauma.

differentials.condition: Migraine with aura, functional disorder, tumour, subdural haematoma

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low glucose mimics stroke; high glucose worsens outcome.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and activate stroke code
actions: ROSIER in the ED; establish time last known well; check glucose.
Immediate non-contrast CT for thrombolysis/thrombectomy candidates; CTA if thrombectomy possible.
Admit directly to an acute stroke unit after assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: IV thrombolysis (haemorrhage excluded)
actions: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg): 10% IV bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min. Standard dose over low dose (ESO).

Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single IV bolus is suggested over alteplase for large vessel occlusion when IVT is given before thrombectomy (ESO); NICE TA990 recommends tenecteplase as an option within 4.5 h.
BP must be 185/110 mmHg or lower before and maintained for 24 h; persistently above despite treatment → no IVT.

4.5–9 h (known onset) or wake-up stroke (within 9 h of sleep midpoint): IVT only with CT/MRI core–perfusion mismatch (or DWI-FLAIR mismatch) and when thrombectomy is not planned; plain CT only → no IVT.
No antithrombotics within 24 h after IVT.
Deliver only within an organised stroke service with trained staff and post-thrombolysis protocols.
VKA with unknown INR → no IVT. Dabigatran within 48 h → idarucizumab then IVT may be considered (ESO, 8/9). Factor Xa inhibitors within 48 h → no andexanet-then-IVT.

clinicalManagement.title: Mechanical thrombectomy
actions: Within 6 h: proximal anterior circulation occlusion on CTA/MRA → thrombectomy plus IVT if eligible.
6–24 h (including wake-up): anterior occlusion with salvageable tissue on perfusion/DWI → thrombectomy.
Posterior circulation (basilar/PCA) up to 24 h with salvageable tissue: consider thrombectomy.
Select pre-stroke mRS below 3 and consider overall status and extent of infarction.

clinicalManagement.title: Antiplatelet if not thrombolysed (after haemorrhage excluded)
actions: Aspirin 300 mg orally (or rectally/enteral tube if dysphagic) daily for 2 weeks, then long-term antithrombotic.
AF with disabling stroke: aspirin 300 mg for 2 weeks before considering anticoagulation.
No routine anticoagulation for acute stroke. Do not start a statin immediately; continue an existing statin.

clinicalManagement.title: Early supportive care
actions: Oxygen only if SpO2 below 95%.
Glucose 4–11 mmol/L.
BP lowering in ischaemic stroke only for hypertensive emergency (encephalopathy, nephropathy, cardiac failure/MI, aortic dissection, pre-eclampsia) or to reach 185/110 for thrombolysis.
Swallow screen before oral intake.

clinicalManagement.title: If CT shows intracerebral haemorrhage
actions: Warfarin with raised INR: reverse with prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K.
Within 6 h and SBP 150–220 mmHg: consider rapid lowering to 140 mmHg or lower, drop no more than 60 mmHg in 1 h (exclusions: structural cause, GCS below 6, early surgery, massive haematoma).
Neurosurgical opinion as indicated.

keyPoints: Time is brain: CT immediately for thrombolysis candidates.
Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% bolus, within 4.5 h.
BP 185/110 or lower before and for 24 h after IVT.
CTA for possible LVO — thrombectomy up to 24 h with salvageable tissue.
Not thrombolysed: aspirin 300 mg within 24 h after CT; swallow screen first.
pitfalls: Giving aspirin before haemorrhage is excluded.
Aggressive BP lowering in ischaemic stroke not receiving IVT.

patientEducation: Stroke warning signs (FAST) and calling for help immediately.
Secondary prevention and AF anticoagulation plan.

mdtReferrals: Interventional neuroradiology for thrombectomy; neurosurgery for ICH.
dischargeCriteria: Managed on an acute stroke unit; swallow assessed; secondary prevention started.
Discharge per stroke team after rehabilitation needs assessed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Secondary prevention (antithrombotic, statin, BP, AF anticoagulation timing); carotid imaging and urgent endarterectomy if 50–99% (NASCET) symptomatic stenosis; rehabilitation; driving advice.
